items.followUp: How does atomic size change across a period from left to right?

rubric.why: This is the stated periodic trend.
rubric.description: States that electropositivity decreases from left to right across a period.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct direction of the trend across a period.

rubric.why: This gives the reason for the trend.
rubric.description: Explains that increasing attraction between the nucleus and outer electrons makes electron loss more difficult.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct explanation based on nuclear attraction or difficulty of losing an electron.

modelAnswer: Electropositivity generally decreases from left to right across a period.
The effective nuclear attraction for the outer electrons increases, so atoms lose electrons less readily.

items.followUp: State the main features of Rutherford's nuclear model of the atom.

rubric.why: The nucleus is the central feature of Rutherford's model.
rubric.description: States that the atom has a very small, dense, positively charged nucleus at its centre, containing most of the atom's mass.
rubric.how: Award up to 2 marks for the small central nucleus and its positive charge/most of the mass.

rubric.why: This describes the electrons' motion in the model.
rubric.description: States that electrons revolve around the nucleus.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for identifying electrons and their revolution around the nucleus.

rubric.why: This adds a further key feature of the model.
rubric.description: States that most of the atom is empty space or that electrostatic attraction holds the electrons around the nucleus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either feature.

modelAnswer: An atom has a very small, dense, positively charged nucleus at its centre; nearly all the mass of the atom is concentrated in it.
Electrons revolve around the nucleus in paths around it.
Most of the volume of an atom is empty space, and electrostatic attraction holds the electrons around the nucleus.

items.followUp: Write any four differences between a mixture and a compound.

rubric.why: Mixture components are not present in a fixed ratio.
rubric.description: States that the composition or proportions of a mixture are variable.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for variable composition.

rubric.why: The components do not lose their individual identities in a mixture.
rubric.description: States that the components retain their individual properties.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this property.

rubric.why: Mixture components can be separated without a chemical reaction.
rubric.description: States that components can be separated by physical methods.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for physical separation.

rubric.why: A mixture does not have the definite melting or boiling point characteristic of a pure substance.
rubric.description: States that a mixture has no fixed melting or boiling point.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either correct statement.

modelAnswer: A mixture has variable composition; its components may be present in any proportion.
The components retain their individual properties.
The components can be separated by physical methods.
A mixture does not have a fixed melting point or boiling point.

items.followUp: Define a coordinate covalent bond and explain its formation in the hydronium ion.

rubric.why: The defining feature is that one atom supplies both bonding electrons.
rubric.description: Defines a coordinate covalent bond as a covalent bond in which both shared electrons are donated by one atom.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that one atom donates both electrons of the shared pair.

rubric.why: Ammonium is a standard example of coordinate-bond formation.
rubric.description: Gives ammonium ion as an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct product/example.

rubric.why: This identifies the donor and the pair it supplies in ammonium formation.
rubric.description: Explains that nitrogen in NH3 donates its lone pair to H+.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying NH3/nitrogen as the donor and H+ as the acceptor.

rubric.why: Hydronium is another standard example of coordinate-bond formation.
rubric.description: Gives hydronium ion as an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct product/example.

rubric.why: This identifies the donor and the pair it supplies in hydronium formation.
rubric.description: Explains that oxygen in H2O donates its lone pair to H+.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying H2O/oxygen as the donor and H+ as the acceptor.

modelAnswer: A coordinate covalent bond is a covalent bond in which both electrons of the shared pair are donated by the same atom.
In the ammonium ion, NH3 donates a lone pair from nitrogen to H+, forming NH4+: NH3 + H+ → NH4+.
In the hydronium ion, H2O donates a lone pair from oxygen to H+, forming H3O+: H2O + H+ → H3O+.

items.followUp: What is an unsaturated solution? Explain how it can be changed into a saturated solution.

rubric.why: A saturated solution contains as much dissolved solute as possible at that temperature.
rubric.description: Defines a saturated solution at a specified temperature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the maximum-solute-at-that-temperature definition.

rubric.why: A supersaturated solution contains more dissolved solute than a saturated solution at the same temperature.
rubric.description: Defines a supersaturated solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the excess-solute definition at the same temperature.

rubric.why: Heating allows more solute to dissolve.
rubric.description: States that the solvent is heated and extra solute is dissolved at the higher temperature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for heating and dissolving the excess solute.

rubric.why: Careful cooling can retain more dissolved solute than the normal saturation amount.
rubric.description: States that the hot solution is cooled carefully, without disturbing it, to obtain a supersaturated solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for careful cooling or preventing crystallization during cooling.

modelAnswer: A saturated solution contains the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve in a given amount of solvent at a specified temperature.
A supersaturated solution contains more dissolved solute than a saturated solution at the same temperature.
To prepare one, heat the solvent and dissolve extra solute until the solution is saturated at the higher temperature.
Cool the hot solution slowly and undisturbed so that the excess solute remains dissolved.

items.followUp: Define a heteroatomic molecule and give one example.

rubric.why: A homoatomic molecule consists of atoms of only one element.
rubric.description: Defines a homoatomic molecule as a molecule made up of atoms of the same element.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the same-element definition.

rubric.why: An example demonstrates the definition.
rubric.description: Gives a correct example of a homoatomic molecule.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for any suitable example, such as O2, H2, N2 or Cl2.

modelAnswer: A homoatomic molecule is a molecule made up of atoms of the same element.
Examples include O2, H2 and N2.

items.followUp: How many particles are present in 0.5 mole of a substance?

rubric.why: This is Avogadro's number, the number of particles in one mole.
rubric.description: States Avogadro's number as approximately 6.02 × 10²³ particles per mole.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct value of Avogadro's number.

rubric.why: This states the relationship between the mole and Avogadro's number.
rubric.description: States that one mole contains Avogadro's number of particles (atoms, molecules or ions).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly relating one mole to the number of particles.

modelAnswer: Avogadro's number, NA, is 6.02 × 10²³ particles per mole.
Therefore, one mole of a substance contains 6.02 × 10²³ particles (atoms, molecules or ions).

items.followUp: What did Rutherford conclude from the deflection of alpha particles in his experiment?

rubric.why: This is one of Rutherford's observations.
rubric.description: States that most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil without deflection.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the observation that most particles passed through undeflected.

rubric.why: This is the other key observation, including the rare large deflections.
rubric.description: States that some alpha particles were deflected and a very few were turned back or bounced back.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct observation about deflected or rebounded particles.

modelAnswer: Most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil without any deflection.
Some alpha particles were deflected through small angles, and a very few bounced back.
